I've set up `main.tscn` (it was already the main scene) as a basic 3D scene. It's saved, and a 5-second test run finished with no errors or warnings. The editor has no window here, so I couldn't take a screenshot; I checked the result by reading the saved scene file instead.

What's under the `Main` root:
- **Cube**: a standard 1×1×1 cube at the origin.
- **Camera3D**: placed at (0, 2, 5) and tilted down about 22° so it looks straight at the cube. It's set as the active camera.
- **DirectionalLight3D**: angled down 50° and turned 30° to the side, with shadows on.
- **WorldEnvironment**: a procedural sky as the background. The scene's ambient light also comes from the sky, and colours use filmic tone mapping.

All of these are ordinary editor changes, so you can adjust them in the Inspector or undo them with Ctrl+Z.

平台跳跃角色做好了，我也实际运行测试过，能正常工作。

在 Godot 编辑器里按 F5 就能直接玩。

Ball now bounces. I added an AnimationPlayer to `res://main.tscn` with a looping animation called "bounce" that plays when the scene starts.

- **The movement:** Ball starts at (200, 200), rises to (200, 150) at 0.5s, and drops back to (200, 200) at 1.0s, at a steady speed. Up is negative y in Godot 2D, which is why the top point is 150.
- **Looping and starting:** the animation is 1 second long, repeats forever, and is set as the player's autoplay animation.
- **Check:** I saved the scene and ran the game for 3 seconds without a window; it reported no errors. The saved file shows the loop, the three positions and the autoplay setting. I didn't watch it run, so the motion itself hasn't been seen on screen.

The keyframes use fixed positions, so if you move Ball later, the animation will still pull it back to (200, 200).

I couldn't add `res://tools/grid_helper.gd` to the project. Scripts marked `@tool` need someone to approve them in the Godot editor. The editor running now has no window, so nobody could be asked, and the write was turned down (`NOT_APPROVED`). I didn't try to get the file in another way.

The finished script is at `/tmp/claude-grid/grid_helper.gd`. I haven't compiled or tested it, because that check runs when the file goes into the project.

**What it does:** it's a `@tool` `Node2D` called `GridHelper`. Add it to a scene and it draws a grid over whatever part of the 2D editor view you're looking at. It redraws when you pan, zoom or resize the view, and it never draws in the running game. Lines stay one screen pixel wide at any zoom. When you zoom far out, the minor lines are hidden so they don't blur together. Settings you can change in the Inspector:
- `cell_size`
- `major_every`: how many cells apart the heavier lines are
- `line_color` and `major_line_color`
- `enabled`

**To get it into the project, either:**
- open the project in the Godot editor with a window and ask me to try again, then approve the prompt that appears; or
- copy `/tmp/claude-grid/grid_helper.gd` into the project's `tools/` folder yourself.

It draws only in scenes you add a `GridHelper` node to. If you'd rather have a grid in every 2D scene without adding a node, that would need an editor plugin under `addons/`. That also needs approval in the editor.

The game now starts without errors.

**Cause:** `main.gd` looked for a child node called `ScoreLabel` (`@onready var score_label: Label = $ScoreLabel`), but the Label in `main.tscn` is named `Score`. That gave two errors at startup:
1. `Node not found: "ScoreLabel"`, which left `score_label` empty (null).
2. `_ready()` then tried to set `score_label.text`, which failed with "Invalid assignment… on a base object of type 'null instance'".

**Fix:** In `main.gd:3` I changed the path to `$Score` so it matches the node. Nothing else in the project used either name.

**Check:** A 5-second headless run of the game reported 0 errors and 0 warnings.

If you'd rather keep the name `ScoreLabel`, you could rename the node in the scene and change the script back.

I added the coin to `res://main.tscn` and saved the scene. A 3-second headless run finished with no errors or warnings. That run only shows the game starts cleanly: nothing touched the coin, so I haven't seen the pickup actually happen.

- **Coin** (Area2D) is a child of `Main`, with the script `res://coin.gd` attached.
- **CollisionShape2D** under it uses a `CircleShape2D` with radius 16.
- **`coin.gd`** connects the coin's `body_entered` signal when the scene starts and removes the coin with `queue_free()` when any body enters it.

A few things to know:
- The coin sits at the scene origin (0, 0) because none was specified, and it has no sprite yet.
- It uses the default collision layer and mask (layer 1), so any physics body on layer 1 will pick it up, such as a CharacterBody2D player.
- There's no player in the main scene yet, so nothing can collect the coin at the moment.

The Player (a `CharacterBody2D` in `res://main.tscn`) is now on collision layer 2 only, and it collides with layers 1 and 3.

- **`collision_layer` = 2**: only layer 2 is on.
- **`collision_mask` = 5**: layers 1 and 3 are on (1 + 4).

I saved the scene, read the values back to confirm them, and ran the game for a few seconds with no errors.

I added a `jump` input action bound to the Space key, and it's now saved in `project.godot` (line 31). The project had no `jump` action before, so nothing was overwritten.

- **Key type:** Space is bound as a physical key, meaning it goes by the key's position on the keyboard, not the layout. That's the usual choice for game controls.
- **Undo:** This change can't be undone with Ctrl+Z in the editor. To remove it, delete the action under Project Settings → Input Map.
- **Editor refresh:** The open editor's Input Map may not show `jump` until you restart the editor. Your scripts can use it right away, for example `Input.is_action_just_pressed("jump")`.

I've ported `res://legacy.gd` to Godot 4 and it compiles now (`gd check` passes). It isn't attached to any scene, so I couldn't run it in the game.

What changed:

| Godot 3 | Godot 4 |
|---|---|
| `extends KinematicBody2D` | `extends CharacterBody2D` |
| `export var` / `onready var` | `@export var` / `@onready var` |
| `var velocity = Vector2()` | removed, because `CharacterBody2D` already has a `velocity` property |
| `velocity = move_and_slide(velocity * speed, Vector2.UP)` | `velocity *= speed` then `move_and_slide()`. "Up" is already the default floor direction, and the engine writes the result back into `velocity` |
| `Color.red` / `Color.white` | `Color.RED` / `Color.WHITE` |
| `yield(get_tree().create_timer(0.2), "timeout")` | `await get_tree().create_timer(0.2).timeout` |

**One thing you might want to change:** the old code multiplied the whole velocity by `speed`, not just the horizontal part, and I kept that. Since nothing ever sets the vertical speed it doesn't matter now. But if you add gravity later, the vertical speed would get multiplied by `speed` again every frame. If you only want horizontal movement scaled, use `velocity.x = (right - left) * speed` instead.

The `$Sprite` path is the same as before. In Godot 4 that node's type is `Sprite2D`, but the path only needs the node's name to still be `Sprite`.

I added the Start button, and pressing it prints "started". I tested it in the running game: firing the button's `pressed` signal printed `started` to the output, with no errors.

What I changed in `res://main.tscn`:
- **`StartButton`**: a new Button with the text "Start", placed at (100, 100) under the root `Main` node.
- **`res://main.gd`**: a new script on the root that prints "started" from `_on_start_button_pressed()`.
- **Connection**: the button's `pressed` signal is connected to that function in the editor, and the scene is saved.

The main scene now has a `Player` node (a CharacterBody2D) that moves in eight directions with the arrow keys at 200 pixels per second. I ran the game, held the right arrow for 0.5 seconds, and the Player moved 100 px (200 px/s) with no errors. I only tested that one direction, not up, down or the diagonals.

**What I added to `main.tscn` (saved):**
- `Player`, placed at (576, 324), with the script `res://scripts/player.gd` attached.
- A child `CollisionShape2D` with a 32×32 rectangle. You didn't ask for this, but Godot warns about a CharacterBody2D without a collision shape, and it lets the Player collide with walls later.

**The script:**
```gdscript
extends CharacterBody2D

@export var speed: float = 200.0


func _physics_process(_delta: float) -> void:
	var direction := Input.get_vector("ui_left", "ui_right", "ui_up", "ui_down")
	velocity = direction * speed
	move_and_slide()
```

- **Diagonals:** `Input.get_vector` scales diagonal input down, so moving diagonally is also 200 px/s rather than about 283.
- **Controls:** the script reads Godot's built-in `ui_*` actions, which are the arrow keys by default, so I didn't change any project settings. They also respond to a gamepad's D-pad. If you want arrows only, you'd need to set up your own input actions.
- **Speed:** it's an exported variable, so you can change it in the Inspector.
- **Visibility:** the Player has no sprite yet, so you can't see it when the game runs.

My first write of the script accidentally used an unrelated platformer script I had left in my temporary folder. I caught it straight away and replaced it with the code above, so the final file is correct.

I added the Hero node to `res://main.tscn` and saved the scene. The game ran headless for 2 seconds with 0 errors and 0 warnings. That run was headless, so I haven't actually watched the animation play on screen.

- **Node:** `Hero` is an `AnimatedSprite2D` directly under the root `Main` node, at position (0, 0).
- **Frames:** `hero_walk.png` is 64×32, which is two 32×32 frames side by side. The node's `SpriteFrames` resource cuts it into frame 0 (x 0–32) and frame 1 (x 32–64).
- **Animation:** `walk` plays at 8 fps and loops.
- **Start:** autoplay is set to `walk`, so it plays as soon as the scene loads.

The sprite is at the scene origin, which is the top-left corner of the screen unless a camera moves the view. You may want to move it somewhere visible.

The floor is in `main.tscn`: a `TileMapLayer` named **Floor** under `Main`, with 20 tiles along the bottom of the screen. I haven't tested a character landing on it yet, because the scene doesn't have one.

- **Tile set:** `res://art/tiles.png` is cut into 32×32 tiles. The sheet only has two tiles, green at (0,0) and magenta at (1,0). I used the green one for the floor.
- **Placement:** The tiles fill cells x 0–19 on row y = 19, so the floor runs from pixel 0 to 640 across and from 608 to 640 down. The window is the default 1152×648, so row 19 is the lowest full row of tiles. That leaves an 8 px gap below the floor and the right half of the screen open. If you want it to reach the edges, I can move it down, stretch it, or change the window size.
- **Collision:** Each tile is solid across the whole square, on physics layer 1. A new `CharacterBody2D` uses layer 1 and mask 1 by default, so it should stand on the floor without any extra setup.
- **Checks:** I saved the scene and ran the game headless for 2 seconds with no errors. The saved file contains the tile collision shapes.

I added a HUD to `res://main.tscn` that shows "Score: 0" in the top-left corner. I saved the scene and ran it for 3 seconds without a window, with no errors or warnings. Because there was no window, I couldn't see the label on screen or try moving a camera.

```
Main (Node2D)
└── HUD (CanvasLayer)
    └── ScoreLabel (Label)  text "Score: 0", 16 px in from the top-left corner
```

The label sits on a `CanvasLayer`, which is drawn on its own layer and isn't affected by a `Camera2D`. So it should stay put when the camera moves.

I didn't add a script to change the number. When you want the score to update, set `$HUD/ScoreLabel.text` from your game code.

`main.tscn`, the project's main scene, is now a main menu: a "My Game" title with Play, Options and Quit buttons stacked under it in the middle of the screen. The scene is saved and runs with no errors. I couldn't confirm the centring by eye: the editor runs without a window, so I couldn't take a screenshot. The test window was also only 64×64, smaller than the menu, so the menu sat at the corner there. The layout is set to fill whatever window it gets and centre the menu, so it should be centred in a normal window.

The node structure:

```
Main (Control, fills the window)
└── CenterContainer (fills the window, keeps its child in the middle)
    └── VBoxContainer (16 px between items)
        ├── Title (Label, "My Game", font size 48)
        ├── PlayButton
        ├── OptionsButton
        └── QuitButton   (each button at least 200×40)
```

The buttons don't do anything yet. When you want them to, I can add a script that starts the game from Play, opens an options screen, and quits from Quit.
